about.title: Corona Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: Corona sits where SR-91 and I-15 meet, and that interchange shapes a lot of the traffic that moves through Riverside County each day. In 2025, the city recorded 735 injury collisions, with 981 people hurt and 2 lives lost. Public records show those crashes cluster on Friday afternoons between 3 and 5 p.m., when commuters heading home mix with local trips along Main Street. Behind each number is someone dealing with pain, missed work, and a phone that keeps ringing with insurance adjusters. LawProactive exists to take one task off your plate. We are not a law firm. We are a free service that connects you with an independent personal injury attorney who handles car accident claims in Corona and works on contingency, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery. California gives most drivers two years to file, but the window against a government entity can be as short as six months, so it helps to get questions answered early. You focus on healing; let a professional handle the paperwork.

items.title: Deadlines are tracked from day one
items.desc: California's two-year filing window feels long until medical treatment drags on, and claims involving a city or state agency can require notice in as little as six months. An attorney can calendar those dates before they become a problem.

items.title: Partial fault does not end your claim
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still recover even if you share some blame for a collision; your share simply reduces the amount. Insurers know this, which is one reason they push for a recorded statement early.

items.title: No fee unless there is a recovery
items.desc: Every attorney in our network works on contingency, and California places no cap on non-economic damages like pain and lost enjoyment of life in ordinary car accident cases. Our connection service is free to you as well.

items.question: The other driver's insurer wants a recorded statement about my crash near the 91/15 interchange. Should I give one?
items.answer: You are not required to give the other side's insurer a recorded statement, and it is generally wise to decline until you have spoken with an attorney. Adjusters may use small inconsistencies to argue you were more at fault than you were. Report the crash to your own carrier as your policy requires, but keep the details brief and factual.

items.question: What evidence should I hold onto after a Corona car accident?
items.answer: Save photos of the vehicles and the scene, the CHP or Corona Police report number, medical records, and any dash-cam footage before it is overwritten. Write down the names of witnesses and note the time of day, since many local crashes happen during the Friday afternoon commute. Keep the damaged vehicle from being repaired or scrapped until it has been documented.

items.question: What if I was partly responsible for the collision?
items.answer: California follows pure comparative fault, so a driver who was 20 percent at fault can still recover 80 percent of their damages. There is no cutoff that eliminates a claim simply because you shared some blame. An attorney can review the police report and evidence to push back if the insurer assigns you more fault than the facts support.
